nodes.label: Vicarious liability: definition and purpose - imposing liability on employer for torts of employee
Justifications for vicarious liability (deep pockets, insurance, control, loss spreading, encouraging safety)
Vicarious liability: three requirements - tort committed, employment relationship, close connection to employment
Employment status test: control test
Employment status test: integration/organisation test
Employment status: multiple/economic reality test (Ready Mixed Concrete v Minister of Pensions)
Modern extension of employment status to 'akin to employment' relationships (Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society; Cox v Ministry of Justice)
Course of employment: torts authorised or closely connected to authorised acts are within course of employment
Course of employment: unauthorised way of doing an authorised act still within course of employment (Century Insurance v Northern Ireland Road Transport Board)
Course of employment: express prohibition does not necessarily take act outside course of employment if act still furthers employer's business (Rose v Plenty; Limpus v London General Omnibus)
Close connection test for intentional/criminal torts (Lister v Hesley Hall)
Application of close connection test to serious wrongdoing (Mohamud v WM Morrison Supermarkets; Various Claimants v Wm Morrisons)
Frolic of their own: acts outside course of employment when employee pursues own purposes (Beard v London General Omnibus; Hilton v Thomas Burton)
Journeys to/from work and detours generally outside course of employment unless employer benefits (Smith v Stages)
Liability for crimes of employees: employer can be vicariously liable for criminal acts if sufficiently connected to employment (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud)
General rule: no vicarious liability for torts of independent contractors
Exceptions to no-liability rule for independent contractors: non-delegable duties, extra-hazardous activities, employer's own negligence in selection (Honeywill and Stein v Larkin Bros)
Contributory negligence: definition - claimant partly at fault for own harm (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945)
Contributory negligence: apportionment of damages according to claimant's share of responsibility (s.1 1945 Act)
Contributory negligence applied: seatbelt/standard of care cases (Froom v Butcher)
Contributory negligence applied: reduced standard expected of children (Gough v Thorne)
Volenti non fit injuria: definition - complete defence where claimant freely and voluntarily consented to risk of harm with full knowledge
Volenti element: claimant had full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk (Morris v Murray)
Volenti element: consent given freely and voluntarily, not under duress or from lack of real choice (Smith v Baker)
Volenti element: claimant's agreement/consent to run the risk can be express or implied by conduct (ICI v Shatwell)
Volenti: rescuers generally not deemed to have voluntarily accepted risk (Haynes v Harwood)
Volenti: limited application to employees due to unequal bargaining power/lack of true free choice (Smith v Baker)
Private nuisance and Rylands v Fletcher: brief recap of the torts these defences apply to
Nuisance defence: prescription - lawful activity carried out for 20+ years without complaint (Sturges v Bridgman)
Defence of statutory authority: activity authorised by statute is a defence to nuisance and Rylands v Fletcher (Allen v Gulf Oil Refining)
Defence of consent: claimant consented to the thing likely to cause harm/nuisance (relevant to Rylands v Fletcher)
Rylands v Fletcher defence: act of a stranger causing the escape, beyond defendant's control (Perry v Kendricks Transport)
Rylands v Fletcher defence: act of God - natural event that could not reasonably be foreseen or guarded against (Nichols v Marsland)
Defence: common benefit - where the thing accumulated benefits both claimant and defendant, no liability under Rylands v Fletcher
Nuisance defence considerations: no defence that claimant came to the nuisance (Miller v Jackson) or that activity is beneficial to public (Miller v Jackson)
Compensatory damages: purpose - restore claimant to position as if tort had not occurred (restitutio in integrum)
Special damages: quantifiable pre-trial financial losses (medical expenses, loss of earnings to date)
General damages: non-quantifiable losses including pain, suffering, loss of amenity, future loss of earnings
General damages: pain and suffering and loss of amenity assessed using tariffs/case comparisons and Judicial College Guidelines
General damages: calculation of future loss of earnings using multiplier/multiplicand approach
Damages payment methods: lump sum award versus structured settlement (periodical payments)
Mitigation of loss: claimant has duty to take reasonable steps to reduce/minimise loss suffered (British Westinghouse v Underground Electric Railways)
Effect of failure to mitigate: damages reduced to reflect avoidable loss
Injunction: equitable remedy ordering defendant to do or refrain from doing an act
Prohibitory injunction: orders defendant to stop committing/continuing the tort (e.g. stop the nuisance)
Mandatory injunction: orders defendant to take positive action to undo the effects of the tort
Injunctions are a discretionary equitable remedy - court considers proportionality and conduct of parties (Kennaway v Thompson; Miller v Jackson)
Damages in lieu of injunction: court may award damages instead of an injunction under Senior Courts Act 1981 s.50 (Shelfer v City of London Electric Lighting Co)
Evaluation: criticism that the Caparo three-stage test for duty of care is unpredictable and gives courts too much discretion (fair, just and reasonable stage)
Evaluation: reasonable man standard in breach is flexible but creates uncertainty in application
Evaluation: causation tests (but-for, multiple causes, Fairchild exception) criticised as inconsistent and policy-driven

Evaluation: Wagon Mound remoteness test provides fairer limit on liability than earlier direct consequence test but 'kind of damage' distinction can be arbitrary (Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton)
Evaluation: psychiatric injury rules (primary/secondary victim distinction, Alcock control mechanisms) criticised as arbitrary and unfair
Evaluation: exclusion of pure economic loss and policy limits (Hedley Byrne exception) criticised as inconsistent
Evaluation: Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 provides good protection for lawful visitors but definitions (e.g. 'reasonably safe', warnings) leave uncertainty
Evaluation: Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 sets a deliberately high threshold for trespassers, criticised for under-protecting vulnerable trespassers (e.g. children)
Evaluation: private nuisance's reliance on 'reasonable use' balancing test creates unpredictability of outcome
Evaluation: locality/character of neighbourhood factor criticised as favouring established industrial defendants over new residents
Evaluation: narrow scope of Rylands v Fletcher (non-natural use, escape requirements) has limited its practical usefulness post-Transco
Evaluation: significant overlap between Rylands v Fletcher and negligence/nuisance raises question whether tort is still needed
Evaluation: vicarious liability promotes fairness to claimants by ensuring solvent defendant, spreading loss via insurance
Evaluation: vicarious liability can be unfair to employers held liable for unforeseeable/serious wrongdoing they could not have prevented (criticism of close connection test post-Mohamud)
Evaluation: employment status tests and 'akin to employment' extension create uncertainty over who counts as an employer
Reform proposals: suggestions for statutory clarification/codification of tort principles (e.g. duty of care, nuisance defences, vicarious liability tests) to improve certainty
